0.title: The Road Between Two Ditches
0.essay:
Some Christians lie awake running through every way tomorrow could go wrong. Others shrug at a real problem, say, “God’s in control,” and leave the letter unopened. Both have missed something. If you have ever wondered how much is down to you and how much is down to God, this study is for you.

Two ditches

Picture a country road with a ditch on either side. The first ditch is passivity dressed as faith. It says, “Whatever will be, will be. God is sovereign, so it does not much matter what I do.” It sounds humble, but it is closer to fatalism than to the Bible, and it often hides fear or a wish not to be responsible. The sluggard in Proverbs had a field “all overgrown with thorns” (Proverbs 24:31), and no amount of talk about providence would have weeded it.

The second ditch is anxious control dressed as responsibility. It says, “If I do not hold this together, nobody will. If I stop watching, it will all go wrong.” It looks diligent and is often admired. But it is exhausting, and it quietly puts us in a place that belongs to God alone. Many conscientious Christians live here, never doubting God in words, yet living as if everything depends on them.

The road between

The Bible’s road runs between them, and it can be put simply: do what God gives you to do, and trust him with what only he can do. When Israel’s army faced two enemies at once, Joab said to his brother, “Be of good courage, and let us be courageous for our people, and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good to him” (2 Samuel 10:12). Joab was no saint, but there it is: fight hard, and leave the result with God.

This is not a partnership in which we do half and God does half. God rules all of it, our part included. The freedom comes from knowing which is which.

Related studies

The studies The Sovereignty of God and The Providence of God set out the doctrine beneath this one; Contentment & Anxiety deals with worry, and Knowing God’s Will with decisions. This study builds on them rather than repeating them.

The chapters

Why We Want Control; My Times Are in Your Hand; Pray, and Set a Guard; What Is Yours and What Is His; The One Who Let Go for Us; and In the Moment and Afterwards.

For reflection

Which ditch do you tend to drift towards: passivity or anxious control? Where in your life right now are you unsure what is your part and what is God’s?

1.title: Why We Want Control
1.essay:
Nobody wakes up and decides to be controlling. It creeps in through love, through fear, through hard experience. We have seen what happens when things go wrong, and we resolve: not again, not on my watch.

What it looks like

The need for control rarely calls itself that. It calls itself being organised, careful, the one who cares. Here are some of its signs.

Worry. The mind runs ahead into tomorrow, rehearsing disasters and trying to solve problems that have not happened yet. Rigidity. A change of plan, and something in you tightens out of all proportion. Over-planning. Every possibility covered, every list checked twice, and still no peace. Managing people. Rewriting someone else’s email, checking up, giving advice nobody asked for, finding it almost impossible to delegate. Being unable to rest. Even on holiday or on a Sunday afternoon the mind keeps working, because stopping feels dangerous.

Martha is a gentle picture of it. With Jesus in her home she burst out, “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then to help me” (Luke 10:40). She was trying to manage the evening, her sister and even her guest. Jesus answered kindly, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary” (Luke 10:41–42).

Why we reach for the wheel

There are understandable reasons. We want to be safe. The world is dangerous, and control feels like protection. We want to secure good outcomes: a healthy family, a steady income, children who turn out well. Some of us learned early, in a chaotic home or a sudden crisis, that if we did not hold things together nobody would. Control was how we survived, and it has never quite let go of us.

None of these desires is wicked. To want your family safe is good. To plan is wise. The trouble begins when control stops being a tool and becomes a refuge, the place we run to for peace.

The oldest temptation

Go back to the garden. The serpent did not tempt Eve with something plainly evil. He offered her a kind of control. “For God knows that when you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). The lie was that God was holding something back, that he could not quite be trusted, and that she would be safer if she took charge of good and evil herself.

That is the root of the human craving for control. At bottom it is the wish to be God: to see everything, decide everything, secure everything, and depend on no one. It promises freedom and delivers fear, because we are not God. We cannot see the end from the beginning. We cannot make anyone love us, keep a child from every danger, or, as Jesus said, “add a single hour to his span of life” (Matthew 6:27). So the harder we grasp, the more anxious we become. We are trying to hold up a weight that only God can carry.

A functional saviour

Timothy Keller often pointed out that we can believe all the right things about God and yet, in practice, look to something else to save us. He called such things counterfeit gods: good things we have made into ultimate things, and then asked to give us what only God can give. Control is one of the commonest. We say Christ is our Saviour, but what actually calms us at night is the plan, the spreadsheet, the knowledge that every risk is covered. When the plan holds, we feel at peace. When it collapses, we feel lost, because something more than a plan has collapsed.

Scripture shows what happens when people seize control from God. Sarai, tired of waiting for the promised child, said, “it may be that I shall obtain children by her” (Genesis 16:2), and gave her servant Hagar to Abram. It was sensible by the standards of the day, and it brought years of grief. King Saul, waiting for Samuel while his army slipped away, decided he could wait no longer: “So I forced myself, and offered the burnt offering” (1 Samuel 13:12). Both were frightened. Both took into their own hands what God had kept in his. And grasping did not make either of them safe.

An example

A mother of three runs her home like a control room. She tracks her teenage daughter’s phone, rewrites her husband’s emails to the school, and has the family holiday planned to the hour. Then the flight is cancelled at the airport, and she finds herself shaking with a fury that frightens her children. In the hotel that night she asks herself why a cancelled flight felt like the end of the world. Slowly she sees it. The plan was what she had been trusting. It had been her quiet saviour for years.

Naming it is a mercy

God does not show us our grasping to shame us, but to lift a weight we were never made to carry. The study Perfectionism & Self-Condemnation explores a close cousin of this struggle.

Sometimes the need for control becomes something more: intrusive worries that will not leave, rituals of checking that cannot be stopped, a dread that fills the day. That may be an anxiety disorder or obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). These are real conditions, and very treatable. Please see a doctor or a qualified counsellor as well as talking to your pastor. Seeking that help is not a failure of faith.

For reflection

Which signs of control, worry, rigidity, over-planning, managing people or being unable to rest, do you recognise in yourself? What experiences may have taught you that you had to hold everything together? What are you most trying to secure by staying in control? When your plans collapse, what does your reaction show about what you were trusting?

2.title: My Times Are in Your Hand
2.essay:
The cure for the craving for control is not to pretend that nobody is in charge. It is to discover that someone is, and that he is good. The Bible’s great comfort is not that life is under our control, but that it is under God’s.

The LORD establishes his steps

Proverbs holds both truths in one breath: “The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps” (Proverbs 16:9). We plan, and we should. But the last word is God’s. “Many are the plans in the mind of a man, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will stand” (Proverbs 19:21). Even what looks like pure chance is his: “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33).

Paul says that God “works all things according to the counsel of his will” (Ephesians 1:11). All things: the weather, the markets, the diagnosis and the delay. The studies The Sovereignty of God and The Providence of God set this out at length. Here we need only its heart. Nothing in your life is outside his hand.

Sparrows and hairs

Jesus brings this down to the smallest scale. “Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows” (Matthew 10:29–31).

Notice what he calls God here. Not fate, not the universe, but “your Father”. That changes everything. Control is frightening in the hands of a tyrant or a blind force. It is comforting in the hands of a father. Christians do not trust a sovereign machine. We trust a sovereign Father who knows the number of hairs on our heads, and cares about them because he cares about us.

My times are in your hand

David wrote Psalm 31 in danger, surrounded by enemies and whispering. In the middle of it he says, “But I trust in you, O LORD; I say, ‘You are my God.’ My times are in your hand” (Psalm 31:14–15). His times: the length of his life, its turns, its seasons of grief and rescue. They lay not in his enemies’ hands, nor even in his own, but in God’s.

That is a sentence to carry with you. When the test results are late, when the job offer has not come, when your child has not rung: “My times are in your hand” (Psalm 31:15). The waiting is in his hand. The outcome is in his hand. You are in his hand.

All things for good

Paul goes further. “And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose” (Romans 8:28). This does not say that all things are good. Some are very bad. It says that God takes all things, the bad ones included, and works them together for the good of his people. Joseph could say to the brothers who had sold him, “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20).

It is God who works things for good, not our management of them. And the good, Paul says, is that we should be “conformed to the image of his Son” (Romans 8:29). God’s purpose is not always our comfort, but it is always our good.

Why this is good news

Sovereignty on its own would not comfort us. A powerful God who did not love us would be the most frightening being imaginable. What makes his control good news is who he is. He is wise: he sees the end from the beginning and never makes a mistake. He is good: he gives his beloved sleep. And above all, he has shown his heart towards us in Christ. “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). If God gave his Son for you, he will not be careless with the details of your life.

Timothy Keller often made the point that God gives us either what we ask for, or what we would have asked for if we knew everything he knows. You do not have to see the whole picture. He does, and he loves you.

Different views, one comfort

Christians understand God’s rule in different ways. Many Arminian and Wesleyan believers hold that God foreknows and permits all things, and works through them for good, but does not ordain free choices or sin.

This commentary’s view: God ordains whatever comes to pass without being the author of sin, and his plan includes the means as well as the ends, so our choices, our work and our prayers are real and they matter. Yet both sides share this study’s comfort: nothing can happen to God’s children outside their Father’s care.

An example

A retired engineer is waiting for the results of a biopsy. All his life he has solved problems, and here is one he cannot touch. For the first few days he searches the internet late into the night. Then his wife reads Psalm 31 to him at breakfast. He writes “My times are in your hand” on a card and props it by the kettle. He still checks his phone too often. But each time he reads the card he says, “Yes, Lord. Yours, not mine,” and he finds that he can sleep.

For reflection

Do you tend to think of God’s control as comforting or as frightening? Why? What difference does it make that Jesus calls him “your Father”? Which of your “times” do you most need to place in God’s hand today? How does Romans 8:32 help you trust him with details you cannot see?

3.title: Pray, and Set a Guard
3.essay:
If God is in control, why should I do anything? It is an old question, and the Bible’s answer is clear: because God works through means. He does not usually act instead of us. He acts through us. Trust in his rule does not make us passive. It frees us to act without fear.

We prayed, and set a guard

When Nehemiah was rebuilding Jerusalem’s walls, his enemies plotted to attack. What did he do? “And we prayed to our God and set a guard as a protection against them day and night” (Nehemiah 4:9). Not prayer instead of a guard, nor a guard instead of prayer. Both. He prayed because only God could protect the city. He set a guard because God had given him eyes, men and spears.

Proverbs says the same. “The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD” (Proverbs 21:31). Get the horse ready, and know that God decides the battle. Preparation is our part. Victory is his.

Paul in the storm

One of the most striking scenes in the Bible is Paul’s shipwreck. After days of storm, all hope was gone. Then Paul stood up with a promise. An angel had told him, “God has granted you all those who sail with you” (Acts 27:24). Paul said, “I have faith in God that it will be exactly as I have been told” (Acts 27:25). Every person on board would live. God had said so.

Then some sailors tried to slip away in the ship’s boat. And Paul, the man of faith, said to the centurion, “Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved” (Acts 27:31). Was that a contradiction? Had God promised or not? Paul saw no contradiction at all. God had promised the end, and God had also appointed the means: the sailors were needed to bring the ship to land. A little later Paul urged everyone to eat: “For it will give you strength, for not a hair is to perish from the head of any of you” (Acts 27:34). Eat, because you will survive. Eat, so that you will survive. Faith in God’s promise made Paul more practical, not less.

That is the Reformed teaching on providence in a single scene. God’s plan includes the means as well as the end. If he has planned that you will recover from an illness, he may well have planned that you will see a doctor and take the medicine.

Work it out, for God works in you

Paul gives the deepest form of this in Philippians: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13). Notice the word “for”. We work because God works. His working does not cancel ours; it is the reason ours is not in vain.

Planning is not unbelief

Some sincere Christians feel guilty when they plan, save, insure their homes or prepare for the future, as if it showed a lack of trust. Scripture does not think so. “Go to the ant, O sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise” (Proverbs 6:6). The ant “prepares her bread in summer” (Proverbs 6:8). “The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it” (Proverbs 22:3).

Planning becomes a problem only when we trust the plan rather than the God who gave us minds to plan with. Jesus pictured a farmer who sows his seed and then “sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how” (Mark 4:27). He does not lie awake willing the seed to grow. Nor does he leave the field unsown and call it faith.

Trusting God never means refusing help

This needs saying plainly. Trusting God never means refusing medical care, ignoring a symptom or staying in danger. To see a doctor, take medicine, lock the door at night or leave an unsafe home is not unbelief. It is using the means God has given, and he has given us doctors, nurses and medicine. Prayer and treatment belong together, as prayer and a guard did on Jerusalem’s walls.

The other ditch

Passivity can look like great faith. “I’m just trusting the Lord” can sometimes mean “I don’t want to face this.” The letter stays unopened. The hard conversation never happens. Sometimes God does tell his people to be still. At the Red Sea Moses said, “The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent” (Exodus 14:14). But in the very next verse the LORD said, “Why do you cry to me? Tell the people of Israel to go forward” (Exodus 14:15). There is a time to stand still and a time to walk into the sea. Faith listens for which one God is asking for.

An example

A woman in her forties finds a lump and tells no one. “If it’s serious, it’s in God’s hands,” she says to herself, and keeps busy. Weeks pass. A friend from her home group hears of it, reads her Acts 27 over coffee and says gently, “God kept every one of them alive, and they still had to stay in the ship.” That afternoon she books an appointment. Whatever the result, she now knows that going was not a lack of faith. It was faith getting up out of the chair.

For reflection

Where might you be using “trusting God” as a reason not to act? What does Nehemiah 4:9 suggest about how prayer and practical action fit together? How does Paul’s conduct in Acts 27 change the way you think about God’s promises and your responsibility? Is there a practical step, an appointment, a conversation, a plan, that faith is asking you to take?

4.title: What Is Yours and What Is His
4.essay:
The road between the ditches needs one skill above all: telling the difference between what God has given us to do and what he has kept for himself. Much of our anxiety comes from carrying God’s part. Much of our passivity comes from neglecting our own.

Secret things and revealed things

Moses gave Israel a sentence that draws the line: “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law” (Deuteronomy 29:29). Some things belong to God: the future, the hidden reasons for what he allows, the hearts of other people, the outcome of our efforts. Others belong to us: what he has told us to do, today.

The anxious controller tries to own the secret things. The passive person neglects the revealed ones. Freedom lies in handing God the first and taking up the second.

If the Lord wills

James speaks to confident planners, people who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go into such and such a town and spend a year there and trade and make a profit” (James 4:13). His reply is searching: “yet you do not know what tomorrow will bring. What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes. Instead you ought to say, ‘If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that’” (James 4:14–15).

James does not forbid planning. The merchants may still go to the town and trade. He forbids planning as though we held tomorrow in our own hands. “If the Lord wills” is not a charm to add to a sentence. It is a posture: I will plan carefully and hold my plans with an open hand, because my times are his.

Today’s part

Jesus said, “Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble” (Matthew 6:34). He does not say tomorrow will be easy. He says it will have its own trouble, and, we may add, its own grace. God gives strength for today’s part, not for tomorrow’s imagined disasters. Much of our control is an attempt to carry next month’s burdens with this morning’s strength. So ask: what is mine to do today? Do that, and put the rest down.

People you cannot control

The hardest place to learn this is with people we love. An adult son who has walked away from the faith. A husband who will not see a doctor. An elderly parent who refuses help. You can see what they should do. You cannot make them do it.

Here too there is a part that is yours. You can pray. You can love. You can speak honestly, once and clearly, at the right moment. You can keep the door open, and set wise limits on what you will do or allow. But their heart, their choices and their response to God are not yours to control. In Jesus’ parable the father let his younger son go with his share of the estate. He did not chase him to the far country. But he watched the road, and “while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him” (Luke 15:20). That is the posture: open hands and a watching heart.

When control becomes coercion

We must be honest that the urge to control other people can become something serious. Checking someone’s phone, controlling their money, limiting who they see, punishing them when they do not comply: this is not love. It is coercive control, and it is a form of abuse. If you recognise it in yourself, stop, confess it, and get help from your pastor and a qualified counsellor. If you are on the receiving end of it, your safety comes first: talk to someone you trust, and contact the police or a domestic abuse helpline.

Faithfulness, not outcomes

Our part is faithfulness. The results are God’s. Paul says of his work in Corinth, “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6). Each of us plants and waters. None of us can make anything grow. The master in Jesus’ parable does not praise his servant for being successful but for being faithful: “Well done, good and faithful servant” (Matthew 25:21).

Put the weight down

What do we do with the part that is not ours? We give it to God. Peter tells us to humble ourselves under God’s mighty hand, “casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). Paul says, “do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God” (Philippians 4:6). The study Contentment & Anxiety explores these verses. Here, notice that casting is an act. We do not drift into trust. We put the weight down, and when we pick it up again, we put it down again.

An example

A father in his sixties lies awake over his adult son, who drinks too much and has stopped going to church. For years he has lectured, rescued and checked up. One evening he takes a sheet of paper and draws a line down the middle. On one side he writes what is his: to pray every day, to tell his son he loves him, to say once, honestly, what worries him, and to stop paying his debts. On the other side he writes what is God’s: his son’s heart, his choices, his future. He prays over the second column and hands it to God. The next week he picks it up again, and hands it back. It is a long lesson, but he sleeps better than he has for years.

For reflection

Which “secret things” are you trying to carry that belong to God? What is your part today, the next faithful step? Is there someone you are trying to control whom you need to entrust to God, while still loving and praying for them? What would change if you measured your life by faithfulness rather than outcomes?

5.title: The One Who Let Go for Us
5.essay:
We cannot learn to trust God simply by being told to. Trust grows as we see how trustworthy he is. Nowhere is that clearer than in Jesus: in the storm, in the garden and at the cross, where the day that looked most out of control was the day most completely in the Father’s hand.

Asleep in the storm

One evening on the Sea of Galilee a fierce storm arose, “and the waves were breaking into the boat, so that the boat was already filling” (Mark 4:37). And Jesus “was in the stern, asleep on the cushion” (Mark 4:38). They woke him with the question every controlling heart asks sooner or later: “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?” (Mark 4:38).

His sleep was not carelessness. It was perfect trust in his Father. He was truly human, and truly tired, and he could sleep in a storm because he knew whose hands held the wind. Then he rose and said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” (Mark 4:39), and it obeyed. Their terror turned to awe: “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (Mark 4:41). The one who could rest in the storm was the one who ruled it. And he is in the boat with you.

Not my will

In Gethsemane we see trust under the heaviest weight ever laid on anyone. Jesus knew what was coming: the cross, and the cup of God’s judgment against sin. He told his Father honestly what he longed for: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42).

That prayer is Eden turned inside out. In the first garden, our first parents reached for control: we will decide; we will be like God. In this garden the Son of God, who truly was God, laid his own will in his Father’s hands. (The study Knowing God’s Will looks at this prayer for times of decision.) Jesus did not stop caring, and he did not stop acting. When he had prayed, he said, “Rise, let us be going” (Matthew 26:46), and walked forward into the Father’s will with his eyes open.

Nor was he a helpless victim. “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18).

The most out-of-control day in history

If ever there was a day when things seemed to spin out of control, it was the day Jesus died. A friend betrayed him, leaders lied about him, a governor who knew he was innocent gave in to a crowd, and the best man who ever lived was killed as a criminal. It looked like the triumph of chaos and evil.

Yet a few weeks later Peter could stand in Jerusalem and say, “this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men” (Acts 2:23). Both are true. The men were lawless and fully responsible. And it happened according to God’s definite plan. When the church prayed after the apostles had been threatened, they said that Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles and the people of Israel had gathered against Jesus “to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place” (Acts 4:28).

At the moment when evil seemed most free, God was most in control. The worst thing human beings have ever done became the means by which God did the best thing he has ever done: he saved sinners. And from the cross Jesus’ last words were words of trust: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46).

So we can trust him with less

Here is the argument the cross makes to the controlling heart. If God was in control on that day, when everything seemed lost, he is in control on this day too. If he could take the murder of his Son and make it the salvation of the world, he can take your lost job, your child’s wandering, your diagnosis, your cancelled plans, and work them for good. They are real and painful, but they are smaller than Calvary.

The cross shows not only God’s power but his heart. Jesus let go into his Father’s hands so that we could be held in them. He bore the punishment for every grasping, God-replacing act of ours, including all our anxious attempts to be our own saviours. The gospel does not say, stop controlling so that God will accept you. It says, God has accepted you in Christ, so you can stop controlling. You are not your own saviour. You have one, and he has finished the work.

Peter, who watched it all and once tried to stop it with a sword, later wrote that when Jesus suffered, “he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). The Christian life is learning, slowly, to entrust ourselves in the same way, to the same Father, because of what that same Saviour has done. What a Saviour, who would loosen his grip on his own life to take hold of ours, and will never let go.

An example

A young mother sits beside an incubator in a neonatal unit. Her son was born ten weeks early. All her life she has been the capable one, but here she can do almost nothing. One night a chaplain reads Acts 2:23 with her and says, “The day that looked most out of control was the day God was most in control.” She is still afraid. But she begins to do her small part, sitting with him, singing to him, learning to feed him, and at the end of each visit she lays her hand on the incubator and prays, “Father, into your hands.”

For reflection

What does Jesus asleep in the storm tell you about him, and about the storms you are in? In what ways is Gethsemane the reversal of Eden? How does Acts 2:23 change the way you look at events that seem out of control? If the Father held even the cross in his hands, what can you now trust him with?

6.title: In the Moment and Afterwards
6.essay:
Truths about God’s rule and our responsibility are meant to be lived on Monday mornings, in waiting rooms and at kitchen tables. Here are some habits for the road between the ditches: not new rules, but ways of living in the freedom Christ has won.

Plan with open hands

Go on planning. Make the budget, book the dentist, write the list. But hold the plan the way James teaches: “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that” (James 4:15). When the plan changes, and it will, remind yourself that the interruption came through the same Father’s hand as the plan.

Pray the plan

Pray through what you intend to do, tell God what you hope for, and hand him the outcome. “Commit your way to the LORD; trust in him, and he will act” (Psalm 37:5). Praying the plan reminds you who is in charge, and brings your desires into the light, where God can shape them.

Name what is not yours

When anxiety rises, ask two questions. What here is mine to do? And what here is God’s? Say the second aloud: “Lord, this interview’s result is yours. Tomorrow is yours.” Naming it hands it over. Then turn to what is yours, and do it.

Take one faithful step

When you feel overwhelmed, do not try to solve everything. Ask, “What is the next faithful thing?” Then do that one thing. “Sufficient for the day is its own trouble” (Matthew 6:34). Send the email. Ring the friend. God gives strength for steps, not for the whole journey at once.

Rest one day in seven

Rest is a weekly act of letting go. God gave Israel a rhythm: “Six days you shall labor, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God” (Exodus 20:9–10). That command finds its fulfilment in Christ, in whom “there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9). Yet the rhythm of work and rest is still a gift, and many Christians gladly set apart the Lord’s Day for worship and rest. However you keep it, stopping says that the world does not depend on you. The work will still be unfinished. That is the point. God keeps the world turning while you rest: “he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep” (Psalm 121:4). The study Busy, Tired & Restless says more about rest.

Give thanks

Gratitude loosens our grip. Paul joins prayer “with thanksgiving” to the peace that will “guard your hearts and your minds” (Philippians 4:6–7). At the end of each day, name three good things God gave that you did not arrange: a kind word, an answered prayer, a problem that resolved itself.

When things go wrong anyway

Sometimes you do everything right, and it still goes wrong. The business fails. The child leaves. The illness comes. This does not mean you failed, or that God failed. Faithfulness was your part, and you did it. The outcome was always his, and he has not let go of it, or of you.

Be honest with him. “Trust in him at all times, O people; pour out your heart before him; God is a refuge for us” (Psalm 62:8). Grieve what needs grieving. And resist the voice that says, “If only I had controlled it better.” Sometimes there is a lesson to learn humbly. But often you are simply a creature, and creatures cannot hold the world together. That was never your job. The study Disappointment & Waiting walks further down this road.

When you have been passive

You have let things drift: the bills, the health worry, the job search. You have called it trusting God, but you suspect it has been avoidance. There is no condemnation for you in Christ, and there is a way out. When Joshua lay on his face after a defeat, the LORD said, “Get up! Why have you fallen on your face?” (Joshua 7:10). Sometimes the most faithful prayer is followed by getting up. Pick one thing. Open the letter. Make the call. Ask a friend to check how it went. Faith does not only rest. It also rises.

When you need more help

If control has taken over your life, with constant checking, intrusive fears or panic, see a doctor or counsellor; medicine, where prescribed, is no failure of faith. If a relationship has become coercive or frightening, safety comes first. And if your distress ever leads to thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life, please get help now. Call the emergency services (999 or 112 in the UK and Europe, 911 in North America) or a crisis line (Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland, 988 in the United States), and tell someone you trust.

An example

A man runs a small building firm. For years he worked seven days a week and lay awake over cash flow. After a health scare he made three changes. Every Monday he prays through the week’s jobs with his foreman, ending, “If the Lord wills.” He stops work on Sundays, even when it costs him. And each night he writes down one thing that is his to do tomorrow and one thing he is leaving with God. Last spring a large contract fell through anyway. It hurt. But he found, to his surprise, that he was grieving rather than panicking. The firm, and his life, had never been resting on him.

Further reading

Jerry Bridges’ Trusting God, John Flavel’s classic The Mystery of Providence and Timothy Keller’s Counterfeit Gods all repay reading.

You will slip into one ditch or the other again. That is not defeat. Each time you take up your part and hand God his, you are learning to live as what you already are: a child in the hands of a Father who numbers your hairs, rules the wind, and did not spare his own Son for you.

For reflection

Which of these habits would help you most this week? What plan do you need to hold with more open hands? Is there one thing you have been avoiding that faith is asking you to do? What would it look like for you to rest, really rest, one day this week?
